The salesman from Geelong Solar was very helpful and he explained everything in detail. There was no pressure to sign up but a $300 discount was offered if I did. He suggested the best layout for the panels.While I was waiting for the installation (several weeks) my gas water heater failed and I needed to get a new one.I phoned Geelong Solar to ask if I should buy an electric water heater, but they didn't get back to me, so I stayed with gas.When the installers came, they changed the panel layout twice again, without consulting me. They may have been in a hurry to knock off work because they worked through their lunch break.Geelong Solar looked after all the paperwork. The whole process was very smooth.The amount of electricity produced depends on the amount of direct sunlight and how close the sun is to the panels.Clouds reduce the amount of sunlight that reaches the solar panelsIn Victoria, Australia, the sun is closest to the panels on the 22nd of December and furthest on the 22nd of June.Ideally, the sun should be directly over the panels, but because the sun is about 30 degrees above the north horizon in winter and 90 degrees in the summer, then the panels need to be set at about 27 degrees on a north-facing roof for optimum performance.It is more economical to use electricity while the solar panels are producing it because any electricity that is not used will only be credited about 50% of the normal charge by the power company.The largest roof of my house faces west which is not ideal for mounting solar panels. I have twelve panels on the west roof and six on the north roof. This equates to a total of 6 kW maximum output.The highest output in one day for my setup was 40kWh at the summer solstice (22nd Dec.) and the lowest was 14kWh at the winter solstice (22nd June) on clear days.My system cost $9673 in July 2020. Federal Government paid $3003. Victorian Government paid $1888. Victorian loan $1888. Balance I paid when installed $2894. Suntech 330W panels, Goodwee 5kW inverter.I don't use my gas wall heaters anymore.I use my split system air conditioner for heating

Investigating solar systems by firstly understanding your power bills and how they work is fundamental to be able to determine is solar economically worth it. I wanted batteries as well to store power for nightly use. This turned out to be too expensive to be worth the investment by some $20,000. It will take a couple more years for the development of this technology to be viable for residential use I believe. I do want a system that I can add to in time, however. It is complicated understanding the various charges on your power bill as there are 4 different charges and 2 discounts available on mine. You also need to understand your usage as per kw/hour - Our power bills are expensive ie: $1,173 & $723 for the last 2 quarters and I want to reduce this cost. When you do this you can then begin to investigate the solar system and the economics.Get 3 quotes - in my case, they ranged from the power retailer, another company people recommended and then Geelong Solar Energy which was recommended by the website Solar Quotes. Prices and systems recommended varied from $10,000 down to $6,890. You then need to understand panels and what is available in size (I have 20 panels @ 300 watts each totalling 6kw) The inverter system converts this to power in my house and the maximum you can have is 5kw without seeking approval to increase this.
